title: Guillain–Barré Syndrome Secondary to West Nile Virus in New York City
case_prompt: A 65-year-old Hispanic woman presented with a 1-week history of intermittent fever. Three days after an initial emergency visit for presumed pneumonia (treated with levofloxacin), she returned with worsening fever (101°F), generalized weakness, inability to walk, confusion, and difficulty expressing her needs. She denied new constitutional symptoms, sick contacts, recent travel, or animal exposures. Examination revealed crackles in the right middle and lower lung fields. Chest radiography showed increased patchy density at the left lung base, and she was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Neurologic assessment on admission showed a mildly confused patient oriented to person, time, and place; she reported weakness but could move her legs and arms, though she could not lift her arms more than 10 inches. A head CT was unremarkable. On hospital day 2, she was oriented only to person, had a rigid neck, incomprehensible speech but followed simple commands, and showed asymmetric facial droop with greater left arm weakness. A repeat head CT was unremarkable. Later that day, she became unresponsive, required intubation, and was transferred to the MICU. Over the next two days, she developed rapidly progressive ascending paralysis with decreased deep tendon reflexes in all extremities. A lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid with elevated protein and a normal white blood cell count.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Stroke was considered because of new-onset facial droop and arm weakness — “Stroke notification was called, and another noncontrast CT of the head was performed which was unremarkable.”  
2. Bacterial meningitis was treated empirically — “She was started on treatment for suspected bacterial and viral meningitis with azithromycin, ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and vancomycin…”  
3. Herpes simplex encephalitis was suspected — “Acyclovir was also administered due to suspicion of a herpes simplex encephalitis” and later excluded by “CSF serology was tested for … herpes simplex virus which were negative.”  
4. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis was considered — “Dexamethasone and IViG were administered for suspicion of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.”  
5. Guillain–Barré syndrome best accounted for the ascending paralysis, areflexia, and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation — “Considering the unique CSF findings, Guillain–Barré Syndrome (GBS) was considered, and its etiology was invested.”  
6. Electrophysiologic studies confirmed the diagnosis — “Nerve conduction studies and an electromyography (EMG) were performed revealing acute sensorimotor axonal and demyelinating peripheral neuropathy consistent with GBS.”
